passage: Zubin, you said "whatever" about your spelling test. I know that word. When I was nine, in Jabalpur, I had a teacher who shouted at every wrong sum. "Ritu, wrong again!" I'd try, get it wrong, get shouted at. Try harder, still wrong, still shouted at. One day I simply stopped. When she asked for my answer I said "I don't know" before even reading the question. Why try, if trying and not trying ended the same way? It felt almost clever, like I'd found a way to hurt less. It took a different teacher, two years later, praising one right step at a time, before I believed my effort could change anything. So when you say whatever, beta, I don't hear lazy. I hear tired of losing.

qa.q: What would the teacher shout when young Ritu got a sum wrong?
qa.a: "Ritu, wrong again!"

qa.q: Why did not trying feel almost clever to young Ritu?
qa.a: Trying and not trying ended the same way, with shouting, so giving up seemed a sensible way to hurt less.

qa.q: What turning point helped Ritu start trying again?
qa.a: A new teacher two years later who praised one right step at a time, which showed that effort could make a difference.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel hearing "I don't hear lazy"?
qa.a: Zubin may feel understood rather than scolded, and more willing to talk about why the spelling test feels pointless.

grounding: An elder recalls giving up on maths at nine when effort never changed the outcome, making passivity feel sensible.

passage: Dilnaz had one old bicycle, her brother's, too tall for her, and only the narrow lane behind the flats to practise in, between parked scooters. Every evening for two weeks she tried. Every evening she wobbled, scraped a knee or bumped a scooter, and the watchman shouted. Her cousins laughed from the balcony. On Saturday Maria from the next building came down with her own small bike. "Want to try mine? It's lower." Dilnaz didn't even look up from the step. "Whatever. I can't ride. I'll never ride." "You haven't tried this one." "Doesn't matter. I always fall." Maria sat beside her, turning a pedal with her hand. Dilnaz picked at the scab on her knee and stared at the gutter.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz practise riding?
qa.a: In the narrow lane behind the flats, between parked scooters.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz refuse Maria's lower bike without even looking up?
qa.a: After two weeks of falling, shouting and laughter, she had come to believe nothing she did would work, so trying again felt pointless.

qa.q: What small choice could help Dilnaz try again?
qa.a: Trying Maria's lower bike for just one push somewhere quieter, so she has a real chance of success that proves effort can work.

qa.q: How might Maria feel sitting beside Dilnaz?
qa.a: Maria probably wants to help and may feel a little hurt by the "whatever", but sitting close shows she hasn't given up on Dilnaz.

grounding: A child who kept failing on a too-tall bike in a cramped lane stops trying and says 'whatever'.

passage: In the Lajpat Nagar flat, Simran's English notebook was mostly red. Every essay came back with "careless!" across the top, however long she spent on it. In August she rewrote one three times; it still came back red. So in September she stopped. When her Rekha masi, visiting from Jaipur, asked about the new essay, Simran shrugged. "Whatever. It'll be wrong anyway." She had written two lines and drawn a cat. "Did you even try?" Rekha asked. "Why would I? Trying and not trying get the same marks." Simran said it calmly, as if explaining the weather. Rekha looked through the old essays, saw how neat the rewritten one was, and felt her throat tighten.

qa.q: How many times did Simran rewrite the August essay?
qa.a: Three times; it still came back red.

qa.q: Why does Simran say it so calmly, as if explaining the weather?
qa.a: To her it is a plain fact that effort changes nothing, so giving up feels sensible rather than upsetting.

qa.q: What could Rekha masi do next to help Simran?
qa.a: Point to one specific thing that improved in the neat rewrite, and help her talk to the teacher about what "careless" means, so effort can be linked to results.

qa.q: What does Rekha feel when she sees the rewritten essay?
qa.a: Her throat tightens as she realises Simran worked hard and was still marked down, so the "whatever" hides disappointment, not laziness.

grounding: A child whose repeated effort keeps getting the same red marks stops trying and says it won't matter.

passage:
"Manoj, nets tomorrow? I'll bowl with you."
"Whatever, bhaiya."
Siddharth lowered his phone. "Whatever? You used to beg me."
"What's the point?" Manoj kept his eyes on the TV. "Every time I bowl, Coach says no-ball. I tried a shorter run-up. No-ball. I tried starting further back. No-ball. He shouts, and the whole team laughs."
"So you've stopped?"
"I'm just bad. Doesn't matter what I do."
Siddharth came and sat beside him. "Last Sunday you bowled four good ones to me in the lane."
"That's the lane. That's different."
"Maybe. Or maybe we mark your stride with chalk and sort out the no-ball together. Just ten balls."
Manoj shrugged. "You'll see. Same thing will happen."
But he didn't say no.

qa.q: What does Coach keep saying when Manoj bowls?
qa.a: Coach says no-ball.

qa.q: Why does 'Whatever' feel like the sensible answer to Manoj?
qa.a: He changed his run-up twice and still got no-ball and laughter; when effort seems to change nothing, not trying at least spares him more shame.

qa.q: What choice does Siddharth make, and why might it help?
qa.a: Instead of arguing, he recalls the four good balls and offers a small shared fix, chalk marks and just ten balls, a chance for effort to visibly work.

qa.q: How does Siddharth seem to feel hearing 'Whatever'?
qa.a: Siddharth seems surprised and concerned, since Manoj used to beg to play, and cares enough to put down his phone and sit beside him.

grounding: A child whose bowling keeps getting called and laughed at, whatever he changes, stops trying and says whatever.

passage: When I was nine, my Hemant Mama checked my maths homework every night after his shop closed. I'm Raghav. Every mistake got a sharp tap on the page and "Careless again!" I tried going slower. Still careless. I tried checking twice. Still wrong somewhere, still "careless". After a few months I stopped trying to get them right. I'd write any number and wait for the tap. When Amma asked why I'd gone so quiet, I said, "Whatever I do, it's wrong." It felt true. I'm eleven now, and Amma found me a tuition teacher who marks what I got right first. Last week I got four out of six, and I actually wanted to know what went wrong in the other two. That felt strange.

qa.q: What did Hemant Mama say at every mistake?
qa.a: 'Careless again!'

qa.q: Why did writing any number feel reasonable to Raghav at nine?
qa.a: Going slower and checking twice still brought the same tap and 'careless', so effort seemed useless and guessing at least cost less.

qa.q: What changed for Raghav, and why did it help?
qa.a: A tuition teacher who marks what Raghav got right first; seeing four out of six correct showed that effort counts, so Raghav wanted to fix the rest.

qa.q: What might Amma have noticed that led her to find a new teacher?
qa.a: Amma saw Raghav go quiet and heard 'Whatever I do, it's wrong', and seems to have understood the problem was the constant criticism, not laziness.

grounding: A child criticised for every mistake whatever the effort stops trying, until a different teacher shows that effort counts.
